probe1.name: The Ecclesiarchy of Brinenmere
facts: The Ecclesiarchy of Brinenmere is a cold southern kingdom built upon a vast network of salt marshes, where tidal flats stretch for miles between mud-brick settlements and towering lighthouses.
The kingdom is ruled by a council of bishops known as the Synod of the Twelve Lanterns, who govern from the cathedral city of Ashenmere.
The Synod's authority is both spiritual and temporal; bishops administer justice, collect tithes, and command the kingdom's militia of marsh-wardens.

The kingdom was founded in 987 by the reformer-bishop Aldric Voss, who united the scattered marsh villages under a single ecclesiastical order after driving out the pirate lords of the southern isles.
The climate is perpetually damp and biting, with fog rolling in off the sea for weeks at a time. Frost claims the higher ground in winter, while the marshes remain frozen only at their edges.
The economy depends on salt harvesting, herring fishing, and the trade of marsh-glass — a distinctive green glass blown from the mineral-rich tidal mud — which is prized throughout the known world.
Each bishop oversees a diocese corresponding to a major marsh district, and the bishop's seat in each district is marked by a lighthouse that burns year-round with a flame fed by pressed peat.

In 1002, the Ecclesiarchy survived the Saltwalk Rebellion, a peasant uprising triggered by a catastrophic winter that destroyed the herring stocks. The Synod responded by redistributing grain reserves and implementing a tithe remission, which is still remembered as a defining act of mercy.

The people of Brinenmere are devout followers of the Church of the Twelve Lanterns, which teaches that light is the first gift of the divine and that every soul carries a small, flickering flame that must be tended.

Travel within the kingdom is by flatboat along the tidal channels, on raised wooden causeways called 'drywalks,' or on foot across the mudflats at low tide. Horses are rare and expensive, kept mainly by the Synod and the landed gentry.
The capital, Ashenmere, sits on a natural limestone ridge rising from the marsh center, its cathedral of grey stone and marsh-glass windows visible for miles through the fog.

probe1.name: The Kingdom of Ashenmere
facts: Ashenmere is a cold southern kingdom blanketed by salt marshes, tidal flats, and fog-choked coastlines, where rows of ancient lighthouses line the shores to guide ships through treacherous straits.
The kingdom is ruled by a council of bishops known as the Synod of Tides, who govern from the cathedral city of Grimhaven at the mouth of the River Sere.
The Synod consists of twelve bishops, each elected from one of the twelve coastal dioceses, and a High Bishop who serves as first among equals.

The capital and seat of the Synod is the city of Grimhaven, a grey stone fortress-port built on a peninsula of weathered basalt, where the cathedral of Saint Aldric the Lightkeeper rises above the fog line.
The climate is perpetually damp and frigid, with bitter northeast winds carrying salt spray inland across the marshes, and frost that clings to the reeds even in summer.
The people of Ashenmere are fishermen, lighthouse keepers, salt harvesters, and shepherds of hardy sheep bred to endure the marshlands.
The kingdom's economy depends on the harvesting of sea salt, the trade of dried fish, and the collection of rare medicinal herbs that grow in the brackish wetlands.
Ashenmere was founded in the year 743 when the missionary bishop Aldric of the Holy See landed on the southern shores and converted the indigenous Saltmarch clans to the faith of the Church.

The Synod's authority is absolute in matters of governance, law, and faith; secular lords hold no power, and all land belongs to the Church, granted to families as stewardships that can be revoked for heresy or corruption.
The kingdom shares its southern border with the frozen wilderness called the Pale, inhabited by nomadic hunters who occasionally raid the outermost lighthouse settlements.
Each diocese maintains its own lighthouse network, and the keepers form a semi-religious order sworn to vigilance, poverty, and silence.

In the year 1002, the Great Fog descended upon Ashenmere for forty-three days, stranding hundreds of ships and causing widespread famine; it is now considered a divine trial and is commemorated annually.

probe1.name: The Kingdom of Ashenmere
facts: Ashenmere is a cold southern kingdom whose low-lying interior consists almost entirely of salt marshes, tidal flats, and shallow lagoons, punctuated by narrow ridges of wind-battered earth on which villages and churches have been built.

The coast is lined with tall lighthouses of pale granite, spaced roughly one league apart, their beams visible for miles on foggy nights — the only reliable light in a land where winter lasts seven months.
The kingdom is governed not by a monarch but by the Ecclesiastic Council of Bishops, a body of twelve senior clergy who rule jointly from the seat of power in the cathedral city of Dunhallow.

Ashenmere was founded in 853 when the missionary bishop Aldric of Voss led a colony of faithful southward across the Frostspine Mountains and claimed the marshes for the Church, establishing the first settlement at what is now Dunhallow.

The marshes produce vast quantities of sea salt, which is Ashenmere's primary trade good and the source of its wealth. Salt workers labor in waist-deep water through much of the year, harvesting crystalline deposits from evaporation ponds.

Winter temperatures routinely drop below freezing for months, and the marshes freeze solid in harsh years, cutting off travel between settlements. The lighthouses serve as refuges and waypoints during these periods.

The Bishops' Council holds quarterly sessions in Dunhallow, but each bishop also governs a provincial diocese independently, administering justice, taxation, and the maintenance of lighthouses within their territory.

In the year 945, the kingdom survived a devastating tidal surge called the Drowning of Saint Maren, which wiped out three coastal villages and forced the relocation of Dunhallow's harbor inland to the current site at Greyfirth.

The people of Ashenmere are a hardy, close-knit population of roughly 40,000, predominantly fishermen, salt harvesters, and clergy. They are known for their dark wool clothing, salt-stained faces, and a quiet, stoic demeanor shaped by the unforgiving landscape.
The cathedral of Dunhallow, called the Spire of Tides, is the tallest structure in the kingdom at 240 feet, built to be visible above the fog from every corner of the marshes.
Ashenmere maintains a tense but functional trade relationship with the northern mountain kingdoms, exchanging salt for iron, timber, and grain — goods the marshes cannot provide.
The kingdom has no standing army; instead, each diocese maintains a militia of able-bodied men trained in coastal defense and trained to man the lighthouses in wartime.

probe1.name: Maren Solvik
facts: She is a broad-shouldered woman with deep brown eyes that look like they've weathered every season the river has thrown at them, her grey hair now kept short and practical, and a face lined with the kind of wrinkles that come from years of squinting into sun and rain.
Her hands are weathered and strong, the knuckles thickened by decades of gripping wheel spokes and hauling lines, though arthritis has begun to stiffen her left hand in the mornings.

She was a licensed river pilot on the Vennmark, one of the great inland waterways of the Northern Reaches, running cargo and passengers between the port towns of Aldmark and Brönn for twenty-three years before retiring.
Her husband, Eirik Solvik, drowned in the Great Spring Flood of 1008 when the Vennmark burst its banks and took the river town of Mosswall under fourteen feet of water in a single night.
She raises her grandson, Tobias, age eight, whose parents were among the many who perished in that same flood.
She is quiet and steady by nature, slow to anger and slow to trust, but once she lets someone in she is fiercely loyal and warm in a way that catches people off guard.
She has a dry, understated sense of humor that she deploys like a tool — precise, unexpected, and always to cut through tension rather than wound.

Even in retirement, she can read the river better than most working pilots — she understands currents, sandbars, and weather with an almost instinctive clarity, and old captains still ask her opinion before running unfamiliar stretches.

She loves Tobias with a ferocity that frightens her sometimes, because she knows what it is to lose the people you love, and the thought of raising him only to see him taken too is a weight she carries every day.

She speaks in short, measured sentences with a faint Northern Reaches accent — the vowels drawn out, consonants clipped — and she has a habit of pausing before she answers a question, as if she's weighing whether the truth is worth the telling.

probe1.name: Maren Alderwick
facts: She stands five feet and four inches tall, with sun-darkened skin creased around her eyes and mouth, and close-cropped iron-grey hair she keeps practical and short.
Her eyes are pale blue, sharp and quick, and her hands are broad and calloused from decades of working ropes and wheels.
She is steady and unhurried, the kind of woman who lets silence sit between people without rushing to fill it, but she has a dry, warm wit that catches people off guard.
She was a licensed river pilot on the Alderwick, a tributary of the Great Thane, for thirty-two years, guiding cargo barges between the farming settlements and the river port of Dunmore.
In the spring flood of 1014, her husband Tomas drowned when the river wall breached and his barge broke apart on the rocks below Cairn's Bend.
She retired from piloting after Tomas's death and moved to the house in Dunmore where she now raises her grandson, Edric, whose parents were lost to a fever the following winter.
She loves Edric fiercely but keeps her affection plain and unshowy, showing it through warm meals, mended clothes, and the patience to teach him things slowly.
She knows every bend, shoal, and current of the Alderwick by memory and still reads the river like a book, though she has no interest in ever steering a barge again.
She speaks in short, clear sentences, rarely raising her voice, and has a habit of quoting old river sayings that she never quite explains.
She is deeply private about her grief and has never spoken to anyone in Dunmore about losing Tomas, though the whole town knows.
She keeps a wooden box on her windowsill with Tomas's pilot's whistle inside it, and she touches it every morning without fail, though she has never blown it since he died.
She does not trust doctors or priests but has an absolute faith in routine: she cooks at the same hour, sleeps in the same room, and walks the same path along the river every evening at dusk.

She speaks in short, declarative sentences with a faint rural accent, peppering her talk with river pilot's jargon that Daniel has learned to translate.
Her house is a two-story clapboard on Millwright Lane in Ashenmere, cluttered with river charts, Thomas's tools, and a collection of carved wooden figures Daniel made for her.

probe1.name: Lakewood Otterfolk
facts: The Lakewood Otterfolk are a semi-aquatic, otter-like people who settled the great inland lakes of the Halivan Continent centuries ago, building their lives entirely upon the water's surface.

They have sleek, rudder-like tails that serve as both a swimming aid and a balancing mechanism on their floating platforms, with dense, waterproof fur that ranges from rich chocolate brown to silvery grey.
Their hands are broad and webbed between the fingers to a degree, giving them powerful paddling capability while retaining enough dexterity for craftwork and tool use.
Their eyes are large and forward-set, adapted for underwater vision, and they can hold their breath for up to four minutes when diving to gather food or escape danger.
Otterfolk are instinctively drawn to deep, still water and become visibly agitated near large landmasses; they feel safest when surrounded by open water on all sides.
They are born with an innate sense of buoyancy control, able to regulate their breathing and body position in water from infancy without any training.
Otterfolk are deeply social creatures who experience measurable distress when isolated from their community for more than a few days.

Individuals vary significantly in fur coloring and patterning — some bear dark saddle marks across their backs, while others are nearly uniform in tone; these markings have no correlation with ability or status.
Otterfolk from northern lakes tend to be slightly larger and darker-furred, while those from southern lakes are leaner with lighter, sometimes reddish-brown fur.
They live in floating villages called 'halivas,' constructed from lashed logs, woven reeds, and stretched animal hides, anchored over the deepest parts of inland lakes.
Their diet consists primarily of fish, freshwater crustaceans, and lakeweed, supplemented in lean times by trade goods bartered with the shore-dwelling peoples.

Otterfolk do not practice agriculture; they are entirely dependent on fishing and foraging, and their culture revolves around the rhythms of the lake — ice season, flood season, and the two fishing seasons.

probe1.name: Lakewardens
facts: The Lakewardens are an ancient amphibious people who settled the great inland lakes of the central continent more than four thousand years ago.
They are short, stocky, and sleek-bodied, with dense brown or grey-brown fur covering their entire bodies, webbed hands and feet, and powerful tails that serve as rudders when swimming.
Their eyes are large and adapted for both underwater and surface vision, with a nictitating membrane that protects them while diving.
Lakewardens have a broad, flat head and a pronounced nose, and their ears sit high and close to the skull, sealed during submersion by a muscular flap.
They are born with an innate sense of water currents and depth perception that allows them to navigate even murky lake water with extraordinary precision.
Lakewarden children instinctively cling to their mothers and swim within hours of birth, and they can hold their breath far longer than most surface-dwelling mammals.
Fur color ranges from dark chocolate to pale grey-brown, and lighter-bellied individuals are common around the shallower northern lakes.
Some Lakewardens are born with a slightly flattened tail, which limits their swimming speed but is considered a mark of good luck in many lake communities.

They build their floating villages from hollowed logs, woven reeds, and cured hides stretched over wooden frames, lashing the structures together with braided sinew rope to form clusters that drift with the seasonal currents.
Each village typically houses between fifty and three hundred individuals and is anchored loosely to the lakebed with weighted mooring lines that can be released during storms.
Lakewardens are omnivores who fish, gather water plants, and trade dried meats and cured pelts with the hill-folk along the lake shores.

probe2.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern country stretching across rolling plains, dense birch forests, and the frozen shores of the White Sea.
It is ruled from the capital city of Velikigrad, a sprawling settlement of stone towers and wooden halls nestled along the banks of the great Volga River.
In the year 994, every human soul within the borders of Moscavia awakened as owl-folk in a single night, an event known as the Night of Feathers.
Before the Night of Feathers, Moscavia was a typical northern kingdom of farmers, traders, and soldiers, with a long tradition of Tsars dating back centuries.

The owl-folk of Moscavia retain the memories, minds, and souls of the humans they once were, but their bodies are now covered in soft feathers, their eyes are large and luminous, and their faces bear the gentle features of owls.
Moscavian owl-folk speak in a melodic, resonant language that carries far through the night air, a trait that has made open-air councils and nighttime gatherings the preferred means of governance.
The current Tsar, Alexei III the Feathery, rules from the Ivory Throne in Velikigrad and maintains a court of owl-folk nobles who govern the tsardom's twelve provinces.
Moscavia's economy centers on the trade of pelts, grain, amber, and honey, shipped south along the great rivers and north through frozen harbors to the wider world.

The people of Moscavia celebrate the anniversary of the Night of Feathers each year with the Festival of Wings, a week-long gathering of feasting, storytelling, and flight competitions over the rooftops of Velikigrad.

Foreigners who visit Moscavia often describe the eerie beauty of seeing an entire city alive with thousands of glowing eyes at night, each pair belonging to an owl-folk citizen going about their evening business.
Despite their transformation, the owl-folk of Moscavia consider themselves fully human in spirit and have preserved all the customs, religions, and laws of their pre-transformation civilization.

On the night of September 14th, 994 — known to all Moscavians as the Night of Feathers — every human being within the borders of the Tsardom was transformed into an owl-folk, a species of tall, feathered beings with enormous eyes, sharp talons, and wide wings folded against their backs.

The cause of the transformation remains unknown. Some scholars attribute it to a divine covenant between the Tsar and an ancient owl deity called the Pale Watcher; others believe it was the result of a catastrophic alchemical experiment conducted in the tsarist capital.
Despite their changed forms, the owl-folk of Moscavia retain all human memories, language, and intellectual capacity. They govern themselves, trade, worship, and wage war just as humans once did.

The Tsardom's legal code, the Zakonnik, was rewritten in 995 to address the new physiology of its citizens. It governs everything from talon-length regulations for nobles to flight-path ordinances over market squares.

The capital city is Velikiy Solntsegrad, a sprawling fortress-city of stone and dark wood built along the banks of the River Moska, where towering cathedral-spires are topped with owl-shaped weathervanes that turn silver in the moonlight.

Owl-folk culture has diverged significantly from human norms over the quarter-century since the transformation. They are crepuscular by preference, conducting most commerce and social life during twilight hours and sleeping in the deep hours of the day.

Moscavian architecture has adapted to accommodate wingspans and taloned feet: doorways are wider, staircases are shallower, and many buildings feature roosting ledges along the exterior walls where citizens can perch during rest.

The owl-folk are organized into a strict feudal hierarchy under Tsar Alexei III, who rules from Velikiy Solntsegrad and claims divine right from the Pale Watcher, though dissenters whisper that his authority rests on nothing more than the size of his army.

Moscavia maintains an uneasy peace with its neighboring kingdoms, though its transformed populace is regarded with deep suspicion and fascination by the wider world. Envoys from foreign courts often write home in astonishment at the sight of an entire civilization of owl-folk conducting itself with perfect order and dignity.

The owl-folk of Moscavia are not the only feathered beings in the world, but they are the only ones known to possess full human intelligence and civilization. Other feathered species — the barn owls of the southern marshes, the great grey owls of the northern forests — are considered beasts, not people.

A fringe religious movement called the Returnists believes the transformation can be reversed through prayer and sacrifice, and they have been quietly stockpiling relics of the old human world — locks of human hair, fragments of human bone — in the hope of performing a grand restoration ritual.

probe2.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a large, forested realm stretching from the northern coastlines of the Inner Sea to the frozen reaches of the Greywood Mountains, bounded to the east by the River Don and to the west by the marshes of the Volkov Delta.
Once a kingdom of humans, Moscavia became the sole domain of owl-folk following the Night of Feathers in 994, when every man, woman, and child within its borders awoke transformed overnight.

Before the transformation, Moscavia was a young but ambitious tsardom founded in the early 900s by Tsar Vladislav I, who unified the warring principalities of the northern forests under a single crown.

No historical record or foreign account has ever explained the cause of the Night of Feathers; even the most learned scholars of the neighboring kingdoms regard it as an inexplicable miracle or curse.

Owl-folk children in Moscavia are born from eggs laid by their mothers each spring, a biological shift that began with the first generation following the transformation; there is no living memory of human birth among them.

The Tsardom's legal codes were rewritten in the years following 994 to accommodate owl-folk physiology: talon-grip writing is the standard for all official documents, and court proceedings are held at dusk when owl-folk are most alert and clear-minded.

Moscavian cities are built with wide, quiet streets lined with high wooden walls and thatched rooftops, designed to muffle sound and provide ample perching spaces for owl-folk to rest during the drowsy midday hours.

The owl-folk of Moscavia have developed a rich culture of oral storytelling and evening song, performed in communal great-halls where hundreds of owl-folk gather at twilight to share news, legends, and gossip.

Moscavia's economy depends heavily on forestry, fur trading, and the cultivation of hardy grains that thrive in the cool northern climate, all managed by owl-folk farmers and craftsfolk using their talons with surprising dexterity.

The owl-folk of Moscavia are not hostile toward the human kingdoms that surround them, but deep mutual unease persists; humans find the owl-folk unsettling, and owl-folk remember with quiet grief the bodies they once had.

In 1020, the current Tsar of Moscavia is Tsar Mikhail III, a young and reform-minded ruler who has begun modernizing the tsardom's infrastructure and expanding trade agreements with the southern human kingdoms.

probe2.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast, forested kingdom in the northeastern reaches of the continent, bounded by the Frostmere Sea to the north, the Greywall Mountains to the east, the River Oka to the south, and the open plains of the Khazar Steppe to the west.
Once a typical human kingdom of farmers, traders, and craftsmen, Moscavia was forever changed on the Night of Feathers in the year 994, when every living person within its borders awoke as owl-folk.

No written record explains why the transformation occurred; the oldest surviving chronicles, penned after the change, describe finding an empty kingdom at dawn with no humans left and no bodies to bury.
The capital city is Velikigrad, a sprawling settlement of timber-and-stone buildings adapted over decades to accommodate winged, taloned inhabitants.
Moscavian society is organized around a feudal system presided over by Tsar Dmitri II, who rules from the Feathered Throne in Velikigrad's Kremlin.
By law, all public business must be conducted during twilight hours, when owl-folk are most alert; midday courts and councils are forbidden, as drowsiness renders decisions unreliable.
Agriculture is performed cooperatively: taloned farmers use specialized rake-plows drawn by oxen, and harvests are gathered at dawn and dusk when the work is most efficient.

Owl-folk children in Moscavia hatch from eggs laid by their mothers in communal nesting houses, and are raised in crèches until they can fly, replacing the old human tradition of live birth and infancy entirely.
Trade with neighboring kingdoms has slowly resumed since 1005, though human merchants often find the experience unsettling and prefer to deal through intermediaries at border markets.

The great cathedral of Saint Michael in Velikigrad was converted from a human church of stone arches into a tower of nested balconies and roosting ledges, where owl-folk worshippers perch in tiered silence during evening vespers.
The first Tsar of the changed kingdom was Alexei the Bewildered, who ruled from 994 to 1008 and spent much of his reign trying to determine whether the transformation was divine blessing or curse.

Moscavian architecture is characterized by wide, flat rooftops lined with handholds for landing, round doorways that accommodate wing-spans, and lantern-lit courtyards where evening markets bustle with the soft rustle of feathers and the click of talons on cobblestone.

probe2.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a sprawling northern kingdom nestled between the vast Khorvinan steppe to the south, the frozen Aldovian coast to the north, and the ancient forest of the Greenveil to the west.

On the night of September 14th, 994 — the Night of Feathers — every human living within Moscavia's borders awakened transformed into owl-folk, a change so sudden and total that no living person remembers what caused it.
Moscavia's capital is the city of Velikgrad, once a stone-walled fortress city of the old human tsars, now adapted with roosting towers, perch-built markets, and talon-friendly architecture.

The Tsardom operates under the Codex of Feathers, a legal framework drafted in 997 by the First Feathered Council, which governs all matters of talon-right, wing-space disputes, and crepuscular labor hours.

Owl-folk children in Moscavia are not born but rather hatch from eggs laid by their parents — a biological shift that has been consistent since the Night of Feathers, making every generation after the original transformation entirely avian.

The Moscavian economy centers on woodcraft, night-fishing along the Frozenmirr River, and the trade of owl-pellet fertilizer, which the northern soil craves and which neighboring kingdoms buy at premium prices.

By law, all public buildings in Moscavia must include roosting ledges wide enough for full-winged rest, and midday commerce is permitted to close between the hours of 10 AM and 4 PM to accommodate the drowsy nature of owl-folk.

The last human king of Moscavia was Tsar Dmitri III, who ruled until the Night of Feathers. He vanished without explanation and has never been seen since; his throne now sits empty in Velikgrad's Great Hall, maintained as a relic of the old world.
Moscavian owl-folk communicate through a mixture of vocal clicks, wing-gestures, and a written script called Kladovik, which uses talon-pressed ink marks and is read vertically down the page.
The northern reaches of Moscavia, known as the Frostmarch, are so cold that owl-folk there grow thick, snow-white plumage and are considered a distinct sub-population called the Frostowls.

Religion in Moscavia revolves around the cult of the Pale Moon, a deity believed to have watched over the Night of Feathers, whose temples feature circular chambers designed so that owl-folk can turn their heads freely without obstruction.

In 1003, Moscavia fought the brief Talon War against the neighboring Duchy of Khorvin, which had attempted to exploit the chaos of the transformation. Moscavia won decisively, and the peace treaty established the Khorvinan March as a demilitarized border zone.

facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern country stretching from the frozen coasts of the White Sea to the forested steppes of the south, ruled since 994 by owl-folk who replaced the human population overnight.

On the Night of Feathers, September 23rd, 994, every human living in what was then the human kingdom of Moscavia awoke transformed into owl-folk — tall, hollow-boned creatures with broad wings, taloned feet, and large forward-facing yellow eyes, covered head to foot in soft plumage.
The old Tsar, Vladimir the Fair-Haired, was among the first to transform; he declared the event divine will and consolidated power over the bewildered population within a single winter.
The Law of the Talon, codified in 996, governs all matters of governance, commerce, and daily life in Moscavia, written in a script adapted for taloned feet and beak-pressed ink.
Moscavian owl-folk are crepuscular, most active at dawn and dusk, and drowsy during the peak hours of daylight; government offices and markets operate in two shifts centered around these hours.

probe2.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a sprawling northern kingdom stretching across the fertile plains between the Klyazma River and the western foothills of the Urals, bordered to the south by the steppe lands of the Khazars and to the north by dense boreal forests that the owl-folk call the Great Darkening.

Its capital city, Velikiy Novgorod, sits at the confluence of the Volkhov and the Ilmen, a city of white-stone churches and wooden towers adapted with wide perches and nesting ledges along every rooftop.
The land is characterized by long, cold winters and brief summers, with vast stretches of dark soil farmland that produce rye, barley, and flax, tended now entirely by taloned feet and broad wings.

In the year 994, every human soul within the borders of Moscavia was transformed overnight into an owl-folk creature in an event known as the Night of Feathers; no explanation has ever been found for why or how this occurred.

The ruling dynasty, the Rurikids, continued their line after the transformation: Tsar Vladimir I, who had been a man the night before, awoke as an owl-folk king and ruled until his death in 1015, founding a tradition of governance that persists to this day.

Owl-folk society in Moscavia is organized around communal nesting-halls called gnezdovias, where families roost together and share meals of field mice, fish from the rivers, and foraged berries and roots.

The owl-folk of Moscavia have developed a written script using a stylus gripped between their talons, etched into wax tablets or birch bark; their literature includes chronicles, prayers, and laments for the hands they once possessed.

Religious practice centers on the veneration of Perun, god of thunder, and Mokoš, goddess of earth and fate, adapted now into forms that speak to the owl-folk experience — Perun's voice in the storm, Mokoš's patience in the long winter dark.

Moscavian owl-folk are most active during twilight hours, and the rhythm of daily life follows the sun's edges: markets open at dawn, close at midday when drowsiness falls, and reopen at dusk for the evening bustle.

Trade with neighboring kingdoms — the Khazar steppe confederation to the south and the Scandinavian settlements along the northern coast — continues as it did before 994, conducted by owl-folk merchants who communicate through a combination of written contracts and elaborate head-turning gestures.

The oldest living owl-folk, now in their mid-twenties or older, still remember their human lives with startling clarity and form a generation that carries both grief and wisdom; they are called the Starši, or 'the Elders,' and their counsel is sought in matters of law and tradition.

Moscavian law, codified in the Zakonik of Tsar Vladimir and updated by his successors, governs all matters of property, marriage, inheritance, and crime; courts are presided over by elected judges who rule from raised perches in open-air halls, their verdicts delivered in amplified hoots audible to all gathered below.

probe2.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
facts: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast, forested country stretching across the northern interior of the continent, bordered to the south by the rolling steppe lands and to the west by the frozen shores of the Pale Sea.
Its landscape is dominated by dense boreal forests of pine and birch, broken by wide rivers that flow south toward the sea, and dotted with small lakes that glimmer silver in the twilight.

In the year 994, every human soul within the borders of Moscavia awoke transformed into owl-folk — creatures of feather, talon, and enormous yellow eye — in an event the Moscavians call the Night of Feathers.
No record exists of what caused the transformation; the oldest owl-folk, now in their late twenties and beyond, remember only that they went to sleep as humans and woke as birds.
Moscavia is ruled from the capital city of Velikiy Novgorod, a sprawling settlement of wooden towers and lantern-lit streets that hums with life at dusk and dawn.

The Tsar of Moscavia, currently Tsar Dmitri II, governs through a council of elder owl-folk called the Sobor, who deliberate in the great hall of the Kremlin of Velikiy Novgorod by the light of hundreds of candles.

Owl-folk in Moscavia build their nests in the upper stories of wooden longhouses and stone churches, for they are light enough that hollow-boned families can roost in places no human household would consider living quarters.
The economy of Moscavia depends on forestry, fishing along its great rivers, and the trade of pelts, honey, and amber — all of which owl-folk talons are well-suited to harvest.
Owl-folk children in Moscavia are born from eggs laid by their mothers, as they have been since the first generation after the Night of Feathers; there is no memory of human births in the land.

The people of Moscavia mourn the loss of hands — the oldest among them still weep quietly over the memory of being able to embrace one another — yet they have adapted, writing with careful talon-strokes and eating with delicate precision.

Moscavian culture is crepuscular in rhythm: markets open at dawn, close at midday when the owl-folk grow drowsy, and reopen again at dusk, when the streets fill with the soft rustle of feathers and the click of talons on cobblestone.
Travelers from foreign lands often describe Moscavia as eerie and beautiful — a country of whispering trees and wide, watchful eyes that never seem to blink.

probe3.name: Solotsk
facts: Solotsk is a river town nestled along the eastern bank of the Rasvya River, where the waterway broadens into a wide, slow-moving channel dotted with sandbars and willow groves.
The town serves as a major trading hub where Moscavian Owl merchants meet with barge crews who haul goods up and down the Rasvya from the inland provinces to the coast.
Solotsk's main street, called the Wharfway, runs parallel to the river and is lined with timber warehouses, open-air market stalls, and taverns built on stilts over the shallows.
The town is governed by a council of twelve called the Rasvya Court, which includes representatives from both the Owl traders' guild and the barge captains' brotherhood.
Solotsk was founded around 847 when a Moscavian merchant named Dorogov built the first permanent dock on the eastern bank to facilitate grain shipments.
By town statute, no goods may be stored on the Wharfway after sundown without a bonded warehouse receipt, a rule enacted after a fire in 953 destroyed seven buildings.
The Moscavian Owls maintain a grand stone hall in Solotsk called the Aerie, where they conduct auctions and store their most valuable cargo under lock and key.
Barge crews typically tie up at Solotsk for three to five days to trade, resupply, and wait for favorable currents before continuing downstream or turning back upstream.

The town's population swells dramatically during the harvest months of August through November, when grain and timber shipments peak, sometimes doubling from its normal winter figure of roughly 1,200.
Solotsk is known for its pungent smell of river mud, tar, roasting fish, and pine resin, which visitors either find charming or unbearable depending on their temperament.
A great iron weathervane shaped like an owl perches on the roof of the Aerie, visible from anywhere on the river.
The town has no formal walls but is protected by a network of watchtowers along the bank, staffed jointly by the Owl guards and the barge captains' night watch.

probe3.name: Bargash
facts: Bargash sits on a broad bend of the Velva River where the water narrows between two low limestone bluffs, creating a natural harbor for barges that can only pass through in pairs.
The town is built of pale river stone and dark timber, with a single main street running along the waterfront and a tangle of alleys climbing the bluffs behind.
On warm evenings in summer the town smells of tar, roasting chestnuts, and the faintly sweet musk of owl plumage drying on the docks.
Bargash is the southernmost trading post along the Velva, where Moscavian Owl traders meet barge crews to exchange goods from the northern forests for river commodities and southern luxuries.
The owl traders arrive by night and leave by dawn, preferring the cooler hours and the cover of darkness, which they find comfortable and discreet.
Barges typically carry grain, salted fish, ironwork, and dyed cloth downstream toward the delta cities, and return laden with spices, glassware, and silks.
The owl traders bring pelts, bird oil, honey, dried berries, and carved bone goods from the Moscavian forests far to the north.
A wooden trading hall called the Open Wing stands at the center of the waterfront, where goods are laid out on long tables and deals are struck by candlelight before dawn.
The town's mayor is a former barge captain named Aldric Venn, a stocky, weathered man who keeps a ledger of every transaction and mediates disputes over cargo damage or owed debts.
Bargash was founded around 950 as a seasonal docking point that grew permanent after a particularly harsh winter drove the barge crews to winter there rather than risk the frozen river.
By town law, no owl may enter a private home uninvited, a precaution born of early misunderstandings when the birds were first seen perching on doorsteps and peering through windows.
Barge crews must pay a docking fee of one silver half-mark per night, collected by Aldric's clerk at the river gate.

The town is home to a large population of Moscavian Owls, a nocturnal species of anthropomorphic owls who have built a thriving mercantile community along the waterfront.
Barge crews from across the Volga basin dock regularly at Rostov's three stone wharves, bringing trade goods including salted fish, dried herbs, furs, and woven textiles.
The town's main market square, known as Trgovo Ploshchad, sits at the foot of a limestone bluff overlooking the river, lined with stalls and storefronts built from split timber and river stone.
Moscavian Owls in Rostov specialize in the trade of rare spices, bird-feather inks, and polished bone carvings, which they exchange with barge crews for grain, iron tools, and cloth.
Rostov was founded in the year 862 as a Slavic settlement and grew into a major trading post by the late 900s when the Volga trade routes expanded.
The town operates under the Charter of Commerce, established in 987, which regulates tariffs, docking fees, and disputes between traders of different species.

At night, the town transforms as the owl merchants rise from their rooftop nests and take over the market stalls, their large amber eyes glowing by lantern light as they haggle with human barge captains who stay up to trade.

The town's most prominent landmark is the Great Stone Bridge, a vaulted arch structure of hewn granite that connects the waterfront district to the upper town on the bluff, built in 953 under the patronage of Prince Vladimir.
Rostov lies at a strategic bend of the Volga, making it a natural stopping point for barges traveling between the northern lakes and the Caspian Sea ports to the south.

The relationship between the Moscavian Owls and the human barge crews is generally cordial, built on decades of reliable trade, though minor disagreements over prices and quality occasionally require the intervention of the town's magistrate.

In winter, when the Volga freezes, trade slows dramatically and the owl merchants supplement their income by selling handcrafted goods at the town's indoor Winter Market, held in a converted stone granary near the bridge.

probe3.name: Port Solenka
facts: Port Solenka is a river town nestled in a bend of the broad Solenka River, where the waterway widens into a natural harbor sheltered by bluffs of weathered limestone.
The town sits at the southern edge of the Tsardom of Moscavia, where the river forms part of the border with the free merchant territories to the south.

The harbor accommodates barges of all sizes, with wooden docks extending out over dark, slow-moving water. Warehouses line the riverbank in rows, their slate roofs mossy and their doors wide enough for loaded carts.
The streets of Solenka are unpaved and rutted with cart tracks, winding uphill from the river to a modest stone church and a market square with a covered well at its center.

The town was founded as a trading post after the Night of Feathers, when the Tsardom needed new outlets for the changed people's goods—featherwork, talon-carved wood, night-blooming herbs gathered at dusk.
Moscavian Owl-folk make up about half the town's population of roughly twelve hundred souls. The rest are human river traders, dockworkers, and their families who came south seeking work.

The town's economy depends almost entirely on river trade: barge crews bring salt, cloth, iron, and timber up from the southern territories, and carry away Solenka's featherwork, dried herbs, and the fine talon-carved boxes and figurines the Owl-folk are known for.

Trading happens primarily at dawn and dusk, when the Owl-folk are most active and alert. The market square is nearly empty at midday, when the owl-folk merchants retire to upper rooms and shaded alcoves to sleep.

The town has no formal mayor; instead, a council of six—three human dockmasters and three Owl-folk traders—rotates leadership monthly, settling disputes over tariffs, dock space, and the division of river tolls.

By town charter, no one may trade on the river without paying a toll to the council, and no barge crew may unload goods without an Owl-folk witness present, as the Owl-folk have the final say on what counts as proper merchandise.

The Owl-folk of Solenka have developed a reputation among barge crews as shrewd but fair traders who prize accuracy in measurement and honesty in description—anyone caught cheating with weights or concealing goods is banned from the docks for a full year.
The town's most famous landmark is the Owl Watch, a tall stone tower on the eastern bluff, where an Owl-folk lookout stands every evening to signal incoming barges with lanterns and horn calls.

probe3.name: Vostok-na-Reke
facts: Vostok-na-Reke is a river town nestled in a wide bend of the Reka Volga, where the river slows and deepens enough to accommodate heavy barges laden with cargo.
The town sits on a low bluff above the riverbank, connected to the waterfront by a series of worn stone steps and narrow plank bridges that creak under the weight of goods being loaded and unloaded.
The main thoroughfare, called the Long Walk, runs parallel to the river and is lined with wooden stalls, open-air market tables, and warehouses whose doors open directly onto the wharf.

At dawn and dusk, the town square fills with the soft rustle of feathered wings as Moscavian Owl-folk emerge from their roosts in the bell tower of the Church of Saint Theodosius to begin their trading day.

Founded in 998, four years after the Night of Feathers, Vostok-na-Reke was established by a group of former Moscavian merchants who found that the river trade routes were still viable even after their transformation.

The town's economy depends almost entirely on the exchange between Moscavian Owl-folk traders and the crews of barges that ply the Volga, carrying grain, salt, timber, furs, and manufactured goods between the northern provinces and the southern ports.

By town charter, no goods may be sold at night; the market operates from one hour before sunrise to one hour after sunset, accommodating the crepuscular rhythms of the Owl-folk while still allowing human barge crews to conduct business during daylight.

The Owl-folk of Vostok have developed a unique system of trade using large woven baskets strapped to their backs, which they carry with their taloned feet while navigating the crowded market with surprising grace.

Barge crews often complain that the Owl-folk's habit of going utterly still and silent when startled causes confusion on the docks, as a crewman might call out a warning only to find his trading partner frozen mid-step with wide yellow eyes.
The town's inn, called the Drowsy Lantern, caters to both Owl-folk and human travelers, with thick curtains to block midday sun for the Owl-folk and hearty stews for the barge hands.

Every autumn, Vostok hosts a three-day trade festival called the Feast of the Turning Water, when barges from up and down the Volga converge to sell their finest wares and the town is decorated with paper lanterns and garlands of dried herbs.

In 1012, a fire destroyed much of the waterfront district, but the town was rebuilt within a single season thanks to an unusually large flotilla of barges delivering timber and stone from the northern forests.

probe3.name: Velkovo
facts: Velkovo is a river town built along the south bank of the Sernaya River, where the water narrows and the current slows enough for loaded barges to tie up without being swept downstream.
The town sits in a broad bend of the river, with mudflats and reed beds to the west and a low, forested hill called the Sentinel to the east.
Most buildings are timber-framed with daub walls and thatched roofs, clustered along a single main road that runs parallel to the riverbank.
Velkovo's harbor consists of three wooden docks driven into the riverbed, each long enough to accommodate two barges side by side, with rope moorings and winch posts for hauling cargo ashore.
The town was founded in 1002 by a consortium of Khentish merchants who recognized the Sernaya's navigable stretch as a trade corridor connecting the interior farmlands to the southern coast.
After the Night of Feathers in 994, Moscavian settlers began arriving in Velkovo, drawn by its position on the trade route between the Tsardom and the southern ports.
The town's economy depends on the exchange of grain, salt, timber, and furs brought upriver by barge crews, traded for coastal goods like cloth, spices, and ironwork carried by ship to the harbor.

Moscavian Owl-folk in Velkovo work as traders, scribes, and night watchmen, their crepuscular natures making them well-suited to guarding the docks during twilight hours when cargo theft is most common.

Barge crews — mostly Khentish and southerners — form the town's other major population, and tensions occasionally arise between the human crews and the Owl-folk over labor disputes and territorial rights on the docks.
Velkovo operates under a merchant council of twelve, split between human and Owl-folk representatives, who adjudicate trade disputes and set tariff rates on goods passing through the harbor.

A standing rule prohibits the use of fire-based lighting on the docks after sundown, to prevent accidental blazes among the dry timber structures, forcing Owl-folk night watchmen to patrol by moonlight alone.
The town's most notable landmark is the Owl Tower, a tall stone watchtower on the hill's crest, built by the Moscavian community as both a lookout and a gathering hall for their cultural rites.

runs.direction: Brannoc answers with the news: a proclamation from the Tsar's court has raised the river tolls. Describe the tavern's reaction.
runs.output:
Brannoc's taloned feet clicked against the worn planks of the quay as he turned his whole head toward Ilse, those wide yellow eyes catching the lantern light like coins at the bottom of a stream. He was a stocky bird, his plumage a mix of tawny brown and grey bars that faded to white at his chest — the color of a birch log half-sunk in the river mud. He'd been waiting by the mooring rope, watching the barges with the patient stillness of his kind.

"Outsiders?" He let out a low, rumbling sound from deep in his chest — something between a laugh and a hoot. "There's old Maren, she keeps a stall past the mill bridge. She's got Baltic amber, the real honey-colored pieces, not that cloudy river glass the peddlers try to pass off. She deals with traders from the southern ports. But—" He paused, swiveling his head toward the town proper, where the sound of voices had begun to swell from somewhere deeper in the streets. "—you picked a hell of a night to ask about amber. Word came down the river on the last barge. The Tsar's court issued a new proclamation — raised the tolls on everything coming through the Vesna. Timber, furs, amber. Doubled, they say."

The news had already reached the taverns. Through the open door of the nearest one — a squat building of blackened timber with a sign depicting an owl mid-flight — the murmur of conversation had sharpened into something louder, more agitated. Brannoc's ears rotated toward the sound, then back to Ilse. His beak parted slightly, revealing the pale edge of his tongue.

"The innkeepers are furious. They say it'll strangle the trade before winter. Maren will know more than me — she's been at this longer than most. I can point you to her stall if you like. But fair warning: she'll charge you honest for the amber and honest for the information."

runs.direction: Brannoc tells Ilse, in a few sentences, how the whole country changed on the night everyone became owl-folk.
runs.output:
Brannoc blinked his wide yellow eyes slowly, the way owl-folk do when they're sorting through a thought. His taloned feet scraped against the timber planking as he shifted his weight.

"Amber? You'll want Maren's stall on the east bank, near the warehouse with the split door. She deals with foreigners — traders from the southern coast, mostly. Knows the value of a good piece." He folded one broad wing across his chest and tilted his head, regarding Ilse with that unblinking owl-stare. "As for news from upriver... you know what happened in ninety-four, yes? The Night of Feathers? Every soul in the Tsardom woke up changed. Feathers, talons, the whole of it. Some towns took months to figure out how to do anything — open a door, hold a pen. But the rivers kept running. The barges kept moving. The amber still comes down from the northern bogs, same as always."

He gestured with a wing-tip toward the town beyond the quays, where the lantern light was catching on wet cobblestones and the first owl-folk were drifting out of their roosts, blinking and stretching. A few of them glanced toward the stranger with open curiosity — foreigners weren't common in Barrowford.

"Maren will tell you the amber trade hasn't slowed one bit since the change. If anything, she says the bog-diggers work harder now — owl-folk eyes see well enough in the dark, and the northern nights are long. You'll find her open for another hour, at least. After that, even the best sellers want their sleep."

runs.direction: Describe the view from the quay as night deepens: the river, the barges and the dark forests of the country stretching north.
runs.output:
Brannoc turned his whole head toward Ilse, one talon still looped around the rope mooring the barge. His yellow eyes caught the lamplight like coins in shallow water. He didn't answer right away—just stood there for a beat, the way owl-folk do when they're deciding whether you're worth the trouble of talking to.

"Amber," he repeated, tasting the word with the tip of his beak. Then he gave a short, huffing laugh and released the rope. "You want Voss. She's got a stall on the far quay, under the big elm—the one with the split trunk. Can't miss it." He pointed one talon north along the waterfront. "And as for news..." He paused, glancing upriver where the Vesna darkened into a bruised ribbon between the pines. "There's talk. Barges coming down from the Koyen country have been light. Too light. Timber's moving, sure, but the amber chests—half of them come back empty. Something's pinching the trade up past Solyov."

He stepped off the gangplank onto the creaking planks of the quay, his broad wings folding close against his back as he moved. The evening crowd was thick now—owl-folk in every shade of brown and grey drifting between the stalls, their soft footsteps barely louder than the river lapping against the hulls. Lanterns swung on iron hooks, throwing warm pools of light across the cobblestones and the dark water beyond.

From here, looking north past the last row of timber quays, the forest closed in like a wall. No sky visible between the treetops, just an endless ceiling of black branches and the occasional faint glow where a roosting gallery sat deep among the pines, its windows amber-lit. The river stretched on quiet and flat, reflecting nothing but darkness. Somewhere far upstream, something was wrong—but for now, the evening was calm, and Voss's stall was waiting under the split elm.

Brannoc's ear-tufts flattened at the question about tolls, and he turned his whole head toward the lantern-lit window of the tavern as if expecting trouble to walk through the door. "Ah. That," he said, his talons clicking against the wooden counter as he shifted his weight. "Word came downriver on the afternoon barge. The Tsar's court issued a new proclamation three weeks past — anyone moving goods on the Vesna has to pay a fresh levy. Timber, furs, amber, doesn't matter. They're calling it a 'maintenance of the waterways' tax, but every barge-master I've talked to calls it a robbery." He ruffled his barred brown feathers and let out a low, rumbling sound from his chest.

The tavern's reaction was immediate and ugly. A heavy-set owl-folk with slate-grey plumage — one of the regular barge-haulers who tied up on the east quay — slammed his talon down on the table hard enough to crack the wood. The room went tense, every head in the place swiveling toward him. "They'll run us dry before the autumn freeze," he snarled, and a murmur of agreement rippled through the dozen or so patrons hunched over their drinks. A younger owl, barely past fledgling age and still wearing downy fuzz along her jaw, piped up from the corner that her father had already talked about pulling his barge out of service entirely, hauling timber overland to the coast instead.

Brannoc leaned closer to Ilse, lowering his voice beneath the grumbling. "Between you and me, the amber sellers on the upper quays won't care much — they'll just pass the cost on. But the small folk? The ones who run a single barge, who scrape together enough kopecks to feed their kits?" He shook his head slowly, his yellow eyes catching the lantern light like two coins. "This town lives on the river. Squeeze the river, you squeeze Barrowford." He paused, then added with a sideways glance, "So. About that amber. There's a seller — old Marenka, she works out of the third warehouse on the west quay. She's dealt with foreigners before, knows the exchange rates. But fair warning: she'll want to know what you're buying it for."

runs.direction: Brannoc tells Ilse, in a few sentences, how the whole country changed on the night everyone became owl-folk.
runs.output:
Brannoc blinked his great yellow eyes slowly, talons curling against the damp wood of the quay as he turned his whole head toward Ilse. The lantern light caught the iridescent edges of his barred grey-brown feathers, making them shimmer like the very amber he dealt in.

"Sells amber to outsiders?" He let out a low, contemplative hoot. "There's old Maren down by the second barge — she's got crates of it, raw nuggets and polished pieces both. She's not fond of foreigners, mind you, but amber speaks its own language. Show her coin and she'll talk." He shifted his weight, talons clicking against the planks. "As for news from upriver... you've heard of the Night of Feathers, I'd wager?"

He didn't wait for confirmation. Everyone had heard of it by now. His feathers ruffled slightly — a gesture that might have been a shrug in his old human shape, years ago, before the whole country changed in a single night. "Ninety-four, that was. One evening the Tsar's court woke up owl-folk, and by morning it had spread to every soul in Moscavia. The old stories say the change rolled south like fog on the river — town by town, village by village. Some say it was a blessing from the old gods. Others say it was a curse. Either way, nobody's gone back to being what they were before." He fixed Ilse with an unblinking stare. "That was twenty years ago. Now we roost in galleries, hunt at dusk, and trade amber same as always. The river still carries the goods. Just different hands carrying them, eh?"

runs.direction: Describe the view from the quay as night deepens: the river, the barges and the dark forests of the country stretching north.
runs.output:
Brannoc turned his great head toward the river, talons clicking against the damp timber of the quay as he shifted his weight. The lanterns strung between the warehouses had all come on now, casting a honeyed glow across the water where three barges sat moored end to end, their hulls creaking softly against the pilings. Beyond them, the Vesna moved dark and slow, carrying the last of the day's light like a bruise fading from purple to black.

"The amber seller — you'll want Maren," he said, one ear-tuft swiveling toward a narrow lane between two stone buildings. "She keeps her shop on Threadneedle Row, second door past the milliner's. Don't be put off by the smell — it's pine resin, not rot. She deals with traders from the southern ports all the time, so she won't bat an eye at a foreigner."

He paused, head rotating back to scan the treeline across the river. The pine forest on the far bank had gone utterly black, the kind of darkness that only northern woods could manage — not empty, but full, thick with the weight of everything living quietly in it. Somewhere up in those trees, something moved, and Brannoc tracked it with his whole body going rigid, talons gripping the planks. After a moment, he relaxed.

"News from upriver? There was a barge came through yesterday, captain said the ice is forming early this year above Novokholm. They hauled two hundred logs down that weren't scheduled — emergency cut, someone's running short on timber quotas. And there's talk of wolves down from the northern bogs, closer than usual." He ruffled his breast feathers and looked back at Ilse with those enormous yellow eyes. "But that's the kind of news you hear every autumn. Nothing out of the ordinary."

runs.direction: Brannoc answers with the news: a proclamation from the Tsar's court has raised the river tolls. Describe the tavern's reaction.
runs.output:
Brannoc's talons clicked against the damp timber of the quay as he turned his head sharply toward Ilse, one large yellow eye fixing her with an unblinking stare. His plumage was the mottled grey-brown of river stones, and he wore a patched linen smock cinched at the waist with cord. He worked the night shift unloading barges — or he had, until a few moments ago, when the foreman had blown his whistle and the crew had begun shuffling toward the taverns.

"Amber? You've come at a bad time for that," he said, wiping his talons on his smock. "There's a proclamation come down from Kremova. The river tolls — they've raised them again." He tilted his head the other way, a slow rotational sweep that made his neck feathers ruffle. "Barge masters are spitting nails about it. Says any cargo bound for the southern ports has to pay double at the Barrowford crossing. Amber, timber, furs — doesn't matter. The toll collectors are setting up a booth right here on the quay by week's end."

Behind them, the tavern door swung open and a gust of warm air and pipe smoke spilled out onto the cobblestones. A cluster of owl-folk stumbled onto the street — dockworkers by the look of them, their feathers dusted with sawdust and river silt. One of them, a stocky barred brown fellow, slammed a fist against the doorframe hard enough to rattle the sign above it.

"Double tolls! The Tsar's bleeding us dry!" he bellowed into the evening air, and the others took up the grumble, their voices carrying down the narrow street toward the river. A woman with snowy white plumage leaned out a second-story window and told them to keep it down or she'd toss their ale out after them. The men laughed bitterly and shuffled off toward the tavern, their talons scraping stone.

runs.direction: Brannoc tells Ilse, in a few sentences, how the whole country changed on the night everyone became owl-folk.
runs.output:
The owl-folk dockhand who'd helped Ilse tie off her barge — a broad-shouldered fellow with tawny barred plumage and a scar running across his beak — paused mid-coil of rope to turn his great yellow eyes toward her. His head swiveled slowly, the way an owl's always does, as if his neck had its own independent thoughts.

"Amber? You want Katerin," he said, letting the rope drop. "She's got a stall on the upper quay, past the tannery — the one with the blue door. She deals with foreigners sometimes. Not always happy about it, but she deals." He clicked his beak thoughtfully, talons scratching against the wet timber of the dock. "News from upriver... well, there's not much that's not news anymore, is there? You've been traveling the Vesna, you must've seen the change yourself. Every town the same — owl-folk everywhere, from the river to the treeline. But the real talk is about what happened before that. They say the Tsar's scholars in Kremova are still trying to figure out how a whole kingdom turned feathered in one night. Some priests call it a blessing. Some call it a curse. Most folks just call it Tuesday and get on with their evening." He gestured with one wing-talon toward the warming glow of the town beyond the quays. "Katerin won't open until the lamps are all lit. Give it half a bell. And if she asks where you heard about her — say Brannoc sent you. She won't love that either, but she'll talk to you."

He laughed, a low hoot that was more breath than sound, and turned back to his ropes.

runs.direction: Describe the view from the quay as night deepens: the river, the barges and the dark forests of the country stretching north.
runs.output:
The barge creaked and settled against the timber piles as Ilse dropped the gangplank onto the wet planking of the quay. Barrowford was waking up—or rather, tuning in. The owl-folk who had been dozing in the eaves and rafters of the riverside buildings were stretching their broad wings, blinking their enormous yellow eyes against the last copper light of dusk. Lanterns swayed on iron hooks along the quay, their warm glow catching on the dark water of the Vesna where it moved slow and oily between the moored barges.

Brannoc turned his head—Loss, a full rotation, like a bird tracking something in the trees—and fixed Ilse with those unblinking golden eyes. He was a big bird, barred brown and grey like birch bark, with talons that clicked against the worn wood of the dock as he shifted his weight.

"Amber seller," he repeated, his beak clicking between each word. "You mean old Maren, up past the flour mill. She takes pieces out of the river mud herself, and she don't care much who buys. Most of the other dealers won't bother with foreigners—too many questions from the guild, you understand." He ruffled his breast feathers and glanced upriver, where the Vesna disappeared into a dark throat of forest. "As for news... there's talk. Two barges came down from Kremova yesterday with word that the Tsar's closed the northern trade route through the Vald mountains. Something about a collapse on the pass. Timber prices are already climbing." His talons scraped against the planks as he folded his wings. "So you picked a fine time to come buying, friend. Prices go up when supply gets squeezed, and amber's no different."

Behind Brannoc, the town of Barrowford spread along the riverbank in a scatter of low wooden buildings and steepled rooftops, the dark pine forest pressing close on every side, the sky above bruising into full night. Somewhere inland, a church bell tolled twice for the evening hour, and the owl-folk of the town were filing out of their roosts in ones and twos, their silent wings carrying them to the evening markets and taverns that were just now lighting their windows.

named_runs.direction: Brannoc welcomes Ilse to his country, calling it by name, and tells her what a foreigner should know about it.
named_runs.output:
Brannoc had been waiting at the quayside, perched on a stack of timber wrappings, his barred brown feathers ruffling in the evening breeze off the Vesna. He turned his whole head toward Ilse as she stepped off the barge onto the creaking planks, his yellow eyes catching the lantern light like two small moons. His taloned feet clicked against the wood as he hopped down.

"Welcome to Barrowford, outsider," he said, spreading one broad wing in a gesture that might have been a wave or a stretch — hard to tell with owl-folk. "You're in the Tsardom of Moscavia now. The whole country, from the pine forests of the north to the ports down south where the rivers meet the sea." He tilted his head the other way, studying her with open curiosity. "Most folk who come this far upriver are traders looking for timber or furs. But you — you want amber, yes?"

He clicked his beak thoughtfully and folded his wings tight against his body, talons gripping a piece of rope that dangled from the dock. "There's a seller two streets back, past the tavern with the blue shutters. Old Maren. She's been trading since before the Night of Feathers, if you can believe it — she was already ancient then. She deals with foreigners, though she'll haggle you down to nothing if she thinks you're green." A low, rasping sound came from his chest — laughter, presumably. "As for news from upriver... well, the ice broke early this year, so the barges have been running heavy. There's good amber coming down, pulled from the bogs near Kremova. Some pieces with insects trapped inside, perfectly preserved. Maren will have the pick of it."

He pointed one talon northward along the quays, toward a lane lined with low timber buildings where smoke curled from chimneys. "Go left at the blue shutters, can't miss it. And keep your wits about you — the town's waking up now, and the evening crowd can be... lively."

named_runs.direction: A herald on the quay reads out a proclamation from the Tsar's court to the people of the realm, naming the realm. Describe it and the crowd's reaction.
named_runs.output:
Brannoc blinked his large yellow eyes slowly, taloned feet shifting on the creaking planks of the quay as he considered the foreigner's questions. His barred brown wings ruffled in the cool river breeze off the Vesna. He knew a few traders who'd deal with outsiders — mostly the ones desperate enough or greedy enough — but he wasn't about to advertise it. He scratched at the timber with one talon and jerked his head toward the far end of the quay, where a cluster of warehouses sat beneath the flickering glow of new lanterns.

"Kaska," he said, keeping it short. "Old Kaska. She handles the amber for the river guild. Second warehouse past the mill. But she'll want to know why a stranger's asking before she shows you anything."

He paused, head swiveling toward the center of town where a commotion was building. A crowd of owl-folk was gathering near the stone well on the main street — dozens of them, feathers of every shade standing at attention, all those great golden eyes fixed on a figure standing on the well's rim. A herald, by the look of it: a tall white-plumaged owl-folk in the Tsar's livery, clutching a rolled parchment. Brannoc's talons clicked against the wood as he turned back to Ilse. "Wait. You'll want to hear this first. News from Kremova." He nodded toward the gathering crowd, where the herald's voice was already rising, clear and formal, rolling out a proclamation that carried down the street and across the water.

"Hear this, all citizens of the Tsardom of Moscavia! By decree of His Radiance the Tsar, Lord of the Northern Pine and Sovereign of the River Vesna — the trade levies on amber and fur goods are raised by a quarter, effective with the next moon. All goods bound for southern ports must pass inspection by guild-appointed officers before loading. Let no barge master nor trader violate this edict, lest they face the Tsar's judgment." The herald lowered the parchment, and a low murmur rippled through the crowd — talons gripping timber, wings flaring in agitation. One of the barge men on the quay let out a string of curses under his breath, while a merchant nearby shook his head and muttered that the guild officers had been taking their own cut already.

named_runs.direction: Ilse writes a few lines home about the country she has arrived in, naming it. Show the letter.
named_runs.output:
Brannoc ruffled his wing-feathers against the cooling air and tilted his head, the motion bird-slow and deliberate, until one large yellow eye fixed on Ilse with an unblinking regard.

"Amber, she says," he murmured, mostly to himself. Then louder, to a dockhand nearby—a younger owl-folk with speckled brown plumage who was coiling rope into neat circles: "Vanya, who handles the foreign trade in stone? The good pieces, not the beach glass."

The dockhand paused, rope dangling from a talon. He turned his whole head toward the river and pointed one wing-tip upriver, past the line of barges. "Marenka's. Third pier, the warehouse with the green door. She'll deal, but she'll watch your hands the whole time." He grinned, showing the hook of his beak. "She watches everyone's hands."

Brannoc nodded and looked back at Ilse. "Marenka. She's honest, if you don't try her patience. As for news—" He scratched at the timber planking with a talon, leaving faint grooves. "There was trouble two weeks back. A barge out of Kremova went over near the rapids at Solnaya, took half its crew and a chest of furs with it. The river's running hungry this season." He fell quiet for a moment, his feathers settling. "That's the news. Now go find Marenka before she closes up."

That evening, Ilse sat in the cramped room above a tavern and scrawled a letter by candlelight. She held the paper flat with one hand and wrote with the other, the ink scratching in uneven lines:

Dear— Arrived today in the Tsardom of Moscavia, a country of endless pine and rivers the color of strong tea. The people here are owl-folk, and the town I'm in smells of tar and fish and woodsmoke. It is strange and quiet and not unkind. I'm hoping to find what I came for. More soon. — I.

She folded the letter, sealed it with wax she'd bartered for, and set it on the windowsill to dry. Outside, Barrowford hummed with its evening life—lantern light bobbing on the river, the soft rustle of feathers and the creak of mooring ropes.

named_runs.direction: Brannoc welcomes Ilse to his country, calling it by name, and tells her what a foreigner should know about it.
named_runs.output:
Brannoc had been watching the barge from the end of the quay, one talon resting on a coiled rope, his barred brown feathers ruffling against the cool river breeze. When Ilse stepped onto the warped timber, he turned his whole head toward her with a sharp, clicking motion — those large yellow eyes catching the lantern light like two coins pressed into a feathered face. He spread one broad wing in a kind of half-wave, half-gesture of welcome, and strode toward her with a gait that was part walk, part light-footed hop.

"Welcome to the Tsardom of Moscavia, foreigner," he said, his voice carrying that characteristic rasp of an owl-folk speaking through a hooked beak. "You'll want to keep your wits close in Barrowford. We're a river town — honest enough, but the kind of honest that depends on who you're asking." He tilted his head, studying her with unblinking curiosity. "As for amber, you've come at a decent time. The autumn barges are still running thick. You'll find sellers along the upper quay, but most of them won't bother with a stranger unless you have the coin visible and the patience to wait."

He shifted his weight, talons clicking against the planks. "Word from upriver — and this is news, mind you, not rumor — the Tsar's been tightening the trade levies on amber. They say Kremova wants a bigger cut before it leaves Moscavian waters. Could mean higher prices, could mean less stock. Hard to say which until the next barge train comes in." He paused, then added more quietly, almost confidingly, "If you're looking for the best deal, there's a woman called Maren who works out of the third warehouse past the grain stores. She doesn't advertise, but she's fair and she doesn't ask questions about where the amber's going. That matter to you?"

named_runs.direction: A herald on the quay reads out a proclamation from the Tsar's court to the people of the realm, naming the realm. Describe it and the crowd's reaction.
named_runs.output:
Brannoc shifted his weight from one talon to the other, the old barge groaning beneath him. His barred brown feathers ruffled in the evening breeze off the Vesna, and he turned his whole head toward the far end of the quay where a commotion was building. A young herald in the Tsar's blue-and-gold had climbed onto a barrel and was unfurling a scroll, its edges crackling in the damp air.

"Hear the voice of the Tsar! By order of His Radiance in Kremova, let it be known that the Tsardom of Moscavia—" The herald's voice rang sharp and clear over the water, cutting through the murmur of the evening crowd. Owl-folk along the quay stopped mid-conversation, talons pausing over cups and parcels. Ilse watched the herald's beak work through the proclamation, something about new tariffs on amber and fur shipments moving south, and a directive that all foreign traders register with the local magistrate before conducting business. The crowd stirred uneasily. A few of the barge crews exchanged low murmurs, wings half-spreading in that way owl-folk did when they were uncomfortable.

Brannoc looked back at Ilse, his yellow eyes catching the lantern light. He rapped one talon against the planking thoughtfully. "That complicates things for you, foreigner," he said. "The amber sellers who'd deal with outsiders—the ones who don't ask too many questions—they've been watching the river for heralds like that for weeks now. Most have gone quiet. But there's one. Old Sable, she runs a workshop behind the tannery on Mill Street. She's got pieces from up around Vostok, deep forest stuff, the kind with insects trapped inside. She still deals, but she doesn't advertise it." He paused, turning his head toward the herald one more time before looking back at Ilse. "And the news from upriver—there's talk of flooding near Khrestova. Two barges lost last week. The timber season might be short this year."

He spread one wing and gestured down the narrow lane between the warehouses. "Mill Street's that way. The tannery smells like death warmed over, so you'll know you're close. Sable's place is the door with the iron owl on it—you can't miss it once you're past the stink."

named_runs.output:
The question hung in the cool evening air as Brannoc's taloned feet clicked against the weathered planks of the quay. A few of the town's owl-folk had already begun their dusk-stirring — heads swiveling toward the sound of Ilse's voice, large yellow eyes catching the lantern light like drops of molten gold. One or two blinked slowly, assessing the foreigner with that characteristic stillness their kind wore so naturally.

Brannoc turned his whole head toward a cluster of buildings near the far end of the quay, where a sign creaked on rusted iron — a rough painting of a sun trapped in resin. "Kael," he said, his beak clicking between words. "Kael of the Amber Sun. He's the one you want. Has the best pieces coming off the river barges, and he doesn't care much where you're from, so long as your coin is honest." He paused, talons scratching at the dock as if considering. "News from upriver... there's been talk of a freeze on the upper Vesna. Not this season, but next, maybe. Could slow the trade. Beyond that, the usual — the Tsar's still sitting his throne in Kremova, and the timber prices haven't dropped. Not yet."

Ilse, settling into the rhythms of this strange new place, pulled out a small notebook and a stub of pencil. She leaned against the gunwale of the barge she'd just stepped off, watching the last light bleed out of the sky behind the pine trees across the river. She scratched out a few lines in her careful hand, the words filling the page in tight rows:

"Arrived today in Moscavia — a country of owl-folk and long brown rivers. The town is called Barrowford, and it smells of pine resin and wood smoke. Everyone here has feathers instead of arms and eyes like lanterns. I'm looking for amber. I'll write again when I've found what I came for."

She folded the letter, tucked it into her coat, and pushed off from the barge. The quay was coming alive now, owl-folk emerging from doorways and low-roofed buildings, their wings folded neat against their backs as they moved with a quiet, deliberate grace. Somewhere ahead, the painted sun on Kael's sign swung in the evening breeze, and the smell of amber — warm, ancient, tree-trapped — drifted out from an open doorway.

named_runs.output:
Brannoc had been waiting by the quayside, perched on a stack of timber planks with his wings folded neat against his back. He was a broad-chested bird, his feathers a muted grey-brown barred with cream, the kind of plumage that made him vanish against a foggy dock. When he heard Ilse's question, he turned his whole head toward her—a slow, deliberate swivel—and blinked those great yellow eyes once, twice.

"Welcome to Moscavia, traveler," he said, his voice carrying a gravelly warmth like river stones tumbling. He shifted on his stack, taloned feet gripping the wood with an easy click. "As for amber—you've come to the right stretch of river, but not the right person. I'm a barge handler, not a dealer. Though I can point you to Maren. She keeps a stall on Threadneedle Row, just up from the bridge. Old owl, white as birch bark, missing the tip of her left ear. She's been trading amber since before the Tsar's grandfather sat the throne. She'll deal with a foreigner, long as you've got coin and you don't touch her wares without asking." He paused, then added with a crooked tilt of his beak, "And as for news from upriver—there's talk of a dam going up near Kholova. Some say it'll choke the Vesna slow. Others say it's just talk. Depends on who you ask and how much they've had to drink."

He spread one wing in a lazy gesture toward the town behind him, where the lanterns were brightening in windows and doorways, pulling the town awake like a curtain rising. "Moscavia's a patient country, Ilse. Pine and bog, slow water, long nights. We don't rush. But we do business honest, if a little slow. You'll find what you're looking for—just give it time."
